title: Tupperware wouldn't sell in shops
hook: Tupperware flopped in shops until it was sold at parties in people's homes.
peek: Earl Tupper's plastic boxes had a clever airtight lid, but shoppers did not know how to close it and walked past. A saleswoman named Brownie Wise showed it off at home parties instead, and sales grew so fast that Tupper pulled it from shops.
lede: In 1946 Earl Tupper, an inventor working in Massachusetts, began selling bowls made of a new, flexible plastic. Their lids were modelled on the sealed tops of paint tins, and you closed them by pressing out the air with a soft burp. In shops they sat on the shelf. Customers could not see what made them special, and nobody was there to show them.

bullets.text: To close a bowl you pressed the lid on, then lifted one edge slightly and pushed down, squeezing out air so the lid locked tight. It kept food fresh, but it needed a demonstration to make sense.
Brownie Wise, a single mother near Detroit, was selling the bowls at parties in friends' homes and outselling many shops. Guests could burp a lid themselves, chat, and then place an order.

In 1951 Tupper took his products out of shops entirely and put Wise in charge of a new home-party sales company, based in Kissimmee, Florida. Thousands of women, many of them housewives, became Tupperware dealers.
In 1954 Wise became the first woman to appear on the cover of Business Week. After a falling out with Tupper she left the company in 1958, the same year he sold it.
